samf-senior-2014-r2-02.title: Sum of squares
samf-senior-2014-r2-02.body:
Each square is non-negative, so the sum is zero only if each is zero: $x=3$, $y=4$, $z=5$. Then $x+y+z = 12$.

**Answer: 12**

samf-senior-2014-r2-03.title: Estimate
samf-senior-2014-r2-03.body:
$\sqrt{24}\approx\sqrt{25} = 5$, so $\sqrt{24}-1\approx4$ and $\sqrt{\sqrt{24}-1}\approx2$. The value is about $\frac{30}2 = 15$. More precisely $\sqrt{24}\approx4.899$, $\sqrt{3.899}\approx1.975$, and $30/1.975\approx15.2$, which rounds to 15.

**Answer: 15**

samf-senior-2014-r2-05.title: Order the numbers
samf-senior-2014-r2-05.body:
The median of nine numbers is the 5th smallest. Suppose the median were larger than 8. Then the numbers $3,5,5,7,8$ would all be smaller than it, so at least five numbers lie below the median, which makes it at least the 6th smallest, a contradiction. So the median is at most 8. It can equal 8: if the three unknown numbers are all at least 9, the ordered list is $3,5,5,7,8,9,\ldots$ and the 5th number is 8.

**Answer: 8**

samf-senior-2014-r2-06.title: Equilateral triangle
samf-senior-2014-r2-06.body:
$AD' = AD = 4$ (rotation about $A$) and $\angle DAD' = 60^\circ$. A triangle with two equal sides enclosing $60^\circ$ is equilateral, so $DD' = 4$.

**Answer: 4**

samf-senior-2014-r2-07.title: Prime factorisation
samf-senior-2014-r2-07.body:
$2709 = 3\cdot3\cdot7\cdot43$. Splitting it into three factors greater than 1 means grouping the four prime factors into three numbers, so exactly one pair of primes is multiplied. The options are: $3\cdot3 = 9$ giving $9,7,43$ (sum 59); $3\cdot7 = 21$ giving $3,21,43$ (sum 67); $3\cdot43 = 129$ giving $3,7,129$ (sum 139); $7\cdot43 = 301$ gives $3,3,301$, which repeats a number. The maximum is $3+7+129 = 139$.

**Answer: 139**

samf-senior-2014-r2-08.title: Permutations
samf-senior-2014-r2-08.body:
There are 6 choices for the first place, 5 for the second, and so on: $6! = 720$.

**Answer: 720**

samf-senior-2014-r2-09.title: Fill the gaps, then the last slab
samf-senior-2014-r2-09.body:
Completing the gaps visible in the figure takes 12 blocks, after which the solid is a $6\times6\times4$ cm box. To obtain a $6\times6\times6$ cm cube we still need a $6\times6\times2$ cm slab, whose volume is $72$ cm$^3$, i.e. $\frac{72}2 = 36$ blocks. In total $12+36 = 48$ blocks.

**Answer: 48**

samf-senior-2014-r2-10.title: Add the equations
samf-senior-2014-r2-10.body:
Adding gives $8\cdot2^a = 16\sqrt2$, so $2^a = 2\sqrt2 = 2^{3/2}$ and $a = \frac32$. Then $2^b = 7\sqrt2-3\cdot2\sqrt2 = \sqrt2 = 2^{1/2}$, so $b = \frac12$. Hence $a+b = 2$.

**Answer: 2**

samf-senior-2014-r2-11.title: Count outcomes
samf-senior-2014-r2-11.body:
Choose which die shows the 4 (3 ways); each of the other two shows one of 5 other numbers: $3\cdot5\cdot5 = 75$ outcomes out of $6^3 = 216$. The probability is $\frac{75}{216} = \frac{25}{72}$, so $x=25$.

**Answer: 25**

samf-senior-2014-r2-12.title: Digit sum
samf-senior-2014-r2-12.body:
A number is a multiple of 9 if its digit sum is. The digits are four different digits from $\{1,3,5,7,9\}$, i.e. all five except one; their sum is $25-d$ where $d$ is the omitted digit. This is a multiple of 9 only for $d=7$ (sum 18). So the digits are $1,3,5,9$, which can be arranged in $4! = 24$ ways.

**Answer: 24**

samf-senior-2014-r2-13.title: Find the group
samf-senior-2014-r2-13.body:
The first 8 groups contain $1+2+\cdots+8 = 36$ odd numbers, so the ninth group starts with the 37th odd number, $2\cdot37-1 = 73$, and consists of the nine odd numbers $73,75,\ldots,89$. Their average is 81, so the sum is $9\cdot81 = 729$.

**Answer: 729**

samf-senior-2014-r2-13.title: Pattern of cubes
samf-senior-2014-r2-13.body:
The sums of the first groups are $1,8,27,64 = 1^3,2^3,3^3,4^3$. In general the first $n$ groups contain $\frac{n(n+1)}2$ odd numbers with sum $\left(\frac{n(n+1)}2\right)^2$ (the sum of the first $k$ odd numbers is $k^2$), so the $n$th group sums to $\left(\frac{n(n+1)}2\right)^2-\left(\frac{(n-1)n}2\right)^2 = n^3$. For $n=9$: $729$.

**Answer: 729**

samf-senior-2014-r2-14.title: Extend the sides
samf-senior-2014-r2-14.body:
Let $\angle B = x$, so $\angle ADC = 2x$. Extend $AD$ and $BC$ to meet at $E$. Since $DC\parallel AB$, $\angle DCE = \angle ABC = x$ (corresponding angles). Also $\angle CDE = 180^\circ-2x$, so in triangle $DCE$: $\angle E = 180^\circ-(180^\circ-2x)-x = x$. Hence $DE = DC = 3$ (equal angles $\angle DCE=\angle E$). In triangle $ABE$, $\angle B = \angle E = x$, so $AB = AE = AD+DE = 5+3 = 8$.

**Answer: 8**

samf-senior-2014-r2-14.title: Parallelogram
samf-senior-2014-r2-14.body:
Draw $DE\parallel CB$ with $E$ on $AB$. Then $EBCD$ is a parallelogram, so $EB = DC = 3$ and $\angle DEA = \angle B = x$. Also $\angle EDC = \angle B = x$ so $\angle ADE = 2x-x = x$. Triangle $ADE$ has equal angles at $D$ and $E$, so $AE = AD = 5$. Then $AB = AE+EB = 5+3 = 8$.

**Answer: 8**

samf-senior-2014-r2-15.title: Diagonal entries
samf-senior-2014-r2-15.body:
The entries on the diagonal (row $n$, column $n$) are $1,3,7,13,21,\ldots$: they increase by $2,4,6,8,\ldots$, so the $n$th is $1+(2+4+\cdots+2(n-1)) = n^2-n+1$. For $n=45$ this is $1981$, the last diagonal entry below 2014. Since 45 is odd, the numbers after 1981 go up column 45: 1982 is in row 44, 1983 in row 43, and so on. The number $1981+k$ is in row $45-k$. For $2014$, $k=33$, so the row is $45-33 = 12$.

**Answer: 12**

samf-senior-2014-r2-16.title: Pythagoras
samf-senior-2014-r2-16.body:
Let $O$ be the centre and $Q$ the foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to $OA$ (so $OA$ is perpendicular to the tangent line). Then $PQ = AN = 15$, $QA = PN = 9$, $OQ = r-9$ and $OP = r$. In the right triangle $OQP$: $15^2+(r-9)^2 = r^2$, so $225 = 18r-81$ and $r = 17$.

**Answer: 17**

samf-senior-2014-r2-17.title: Deduce
samf-senior-2014-r2-17.body:
If Dr Richards were guilty, Lady Windermere would be guilty too (first clue), contradicting the second clue. So Dr Richards is innocent, and by the third clue so is Miss Carlyle. Someone is guilty, so it is Lady Windermere (room 36).

**Answer: 36**

samf-senior-2014-r2-18.title: Prime factorisation
samf-senior-2014-r2-18.body:
$14! = 2^{11}\cdot3^5\cdot5^2\cdot7^2\cdot11\cdot13$. A perfect square needs every prime to an even power. The primes 11 and 13 occur only in the numbers 11 and 13, so these must be omitted (otherwise their exponents are 1). Omitting just 11 and 13 leaves $2^{11}3^5$, not a square, so at least one more number must be omitted: $n\le11$. Omitting also 6 removes $2\cdot3$, leaving $2^{10}3^45^27^2$, a perfect square. So $1,2,3,4,5,7,8,9,10,12,14$ (11 numbers) works, and the maximum is 11.

**Answer: 11**

samf-senior-2014-r2-19.title: Ratio of distances
samf-senior-2014-r2-19.body:
Let the circumference be $x$ m. At the first meeting together they have covered half a lap: B rode 100 m and A rode $\frac x2-100$ m. At the second meeting they have covered $\frac32$ laps in total: A rode $x-60$ m and B rode $\frac{3x}2-(x-60) = \frac x2+60$ m. The riders' distances are in a fixed ratio (constant speeds), so
$$\frac{\frac x2-100}{100} = \frac{x-60}{\frac x2+60}.$$
Cross-multiplying: $\left(\frac x2-100\right)\left(\frac x2+60\right) = 100(x-60)$, i.e. $\frac{x^2}4-20x-6000 = 100x-6000$, so $\frac{x^2}4 = 120x$ and $x=480$.

**Answer: 480 m**

samf-senior-2014-r2-20.title: Divisibility
samf-senior-2014-r2-20.body:
The number of balls per box is $\frac{n^2+290n-2490}{n+300} = n-10+\frac{510}{n+300}$ (since $(n+300)(n-10) = n^2+290n-3000$). This must be an integer, so $n+300$ divides 510. But $n+300>300$, and the only divisor of 510 above 300 is 510 itself ($510/2 = 255<300$). So $n+300 = 510$, $n = 210$. (Each box then has $200+1 = 201$ balls.)

**Answer: 210**
